source_policy.generation: Lecture-derived concise medical flashcards; emphasize core mechanisms, relationships, clinical application, and exam-relevant understanding rather than trivia.

questions.stem: Why are RBCs biconcave?

options.A: To increase membrane surface area for efficient gas exchange.
options.B: Hypoxia → ↑EPO → stimulation of erythropoiesis in bone marrow.
options.C: High-value protein supplies globin; iron is required for heme.
options.D: Red marrow of flat bones plus proximal parts of long bones.

questions.explanation: To increase membrane surface area for efficient gas exchange.

questions.stem: Why must the RBC membrane be flexible?

options.A: The percentage of whole-blood volume occupied by RBCs.
options.B: Heme → iron + biliverdin; biliverdin → bilirubin for biliary excretion.
options.C: Anemia/overhydration/pregnancy lower it; polycythemia/dehydration raise it.
options.D: So RBCs can deform and pass through narrow capillaries without rupturing.

questions.explanation: So RBCs can deform and pass through narrow capillaries without rupturing.

questions.stem: What is the normal RBC lifespan?

options.A: Rouleaux formation.
options.B: Tissue hypoxia.
options.C: About 120 days (±7 days).
options.D: Kidney ~90%; liver ~10%.

questions.explanation: About 120 days (±7 days).

questions.stem: How is most CO₂ transported in blood?

options.A: High-value protein supplies globin; iron is required for heme.
options.B: About 70% as bicarbonate; ~20% binds hemoglobin as carbamino-Hb.
options.C: It rapidly supports CO₂ conversion to bicarbonate for CO₂ transport.
options.D: Hypoxia → ↑EPO → stimulation of erythropoiesis in bone marrow.

questions.explanation: About 70% as bicarbonate; ~20% binds hemoglobin as carbamino-Hb.

questions.stem: Why is carbonic anhydrase important in RBCs?

options.A: It rapidly supports CO₂ conversion to bicarbonate for CO₂ transport.
options.B: About 70% as bicarbonate; ~20% binds hemoglobin as carbamino-Hb.
options.C: Heme → iron + biliverdin; biliverdin → bilirubin for biliary excretion.
options.D: No. It is nonspecific and mainly useful as a prognostic/follow-up test.

questions.explanation: It rapidly supports CO₂ conversion to bicarbonate for CO₂ transport.

questions.stem: Why is G6PD important in RBCs?

options.A: They are required for normal maturation of RBC precursors.
options.B: Anemia/overhydration/pregnancy lower it; polycythemia/dehydration raise it.
options.C: So RBCs can deform and pass through narrow capillaries without rupturing.
options.D: It generates NADPH via the HMP shunt, helping maintain normal RBC fragility.

questions.explanation: It generates NADPH via the HMP shunt, helping maintain normal RBC fragility.

questions.stem: What is the main physiological trigger for erythropoiesis?

options.A: Kidney ~90%; liver ~10%.

questions.explanation: Tissue hypoxia.

questions.stem: What is heme structurally?

options.A: An iron-containing porphyrin made of four pyrrole rings linked by methenyl bridges.
options.B: Inserts iron into protoporphyrin IX to form heme.
options.C: Four PBG molecules → hydroxymethylbilane.
options.D: First step + last 3 steps in mitochondria; intermediate steps in cytosol.

options.A: Pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6).
options.B: It suppresses ALA synthase activity.

options.C: First step + last 3 steps in mitochondria; intermediate steps in cytosol.

questions.stem: What converts ALA to porphobilinogen?

options.A: ALA synthase forming δ-ALA from glycine + succinyl-CoA.
options.B: Blood lead level because lead concentrates in erythrocytes.

questions.explanation: ALA dehydratase (PBG synthase); it is inhibited by lead.

options.A: Reservoir of ApoC-II/ApoE and mediator of reverse cholesterol transport.

questions.stem: What is preload in the intact heart?

options.A: More output from one side increases venous return/preload to the other side, raising its stroke volume.

questions.stem: How does sympathetic venoconstriction affect preload?

options.A: It increases venous return → increases EDV/preload.
options.B: Lower ESV and therefore higher stroke volume.
options.C: They increase Ca²⁺ influx and cross-bridge cycling at a given EDV.
options.D: They reduce Ca²⁺ influx needed for excitation–contraction coupling.

questions.explanation: It increases venous return → increases EDV/preload.

options.A: Lower ESV and therefore higher stroke volume.
options.B: The resting initial fiber length, approximated by end-diastolic volume (EDV).

options.D: Muscle pump, respiratory pump, cardiac suction, sympathetic venoconstriction, blood volume, stretchability.

questions.stem: What is heterometric autoregulation?

options.A: Muscle pump + sympathetic venoconstriction increase venous return and EDV → ↑SV.
options.B: The resting initial fiber length, approximated by end-diastolic volume (EDV).
options.C: Increased contractile force caused by increased EDV (Frank–Starling mechanism).
options.D: Within limits, greater initial cardiac muscle length → greater force of contraction.

questions.explanation: Increased contractile force caused by increased EDV (Frank–Starling mechanism).

options.A: Muscle pump, respiratory pump, cardiac suction, sympathetic venoconstriction, blood volume, stretchability.

options.C: Within limits, greater initial cardiac muscle length → greater force of contraction.
options.D: The resting initial fiber length, approximated by end-diastolic volume (EDV).

questions.explanation: Increased contractile force secondary to increased aortic pressure without relying on increased fiber length.
